claims.claim: In the study's Table 8 the syntactic pattern DT NN IN NN CC, represented by sequences such as a mix of pride and or a sense of wonder and, was edited by the writers 54% of the times it occurred.
claims.source: Tuhin Chakrabarty, Philippe Laban et al., Salesforce AI Research, arXiv:2409.14509, September 2024
claims.page: Table 8, first row (Syntactic Pattern DT NN IN NN CC, % of Times Edited 54%)

claims.claim: The study reports that the word unspoken occurs in about 15% of the LLM-generated responses in the LAMP corpus.
claims.source: Tuhin Chakrabarty, Philippe Laban et al., Salesforce AI Research, arXiv:2409.14509, September 2024
claims.quote: a word like unspoken occurs in about 15% of LLM-generated responses

claims.claim: The study reports that the phrases weight of, sense of and mix of occur very rarely or not at all in the human-written seed paragraphs while occurring frequently in the LLM-generated responses.
claims.source: Tuhin Chakrabarty, Philippe Laban et al., Salesforce AI Research, arXiv:2409.14509, September 2024

claims.claim: The study calls it the most surprising finding that all three LLMs generate the same idiosyncratic words and phrases, and suggests overlap in instruction tuning data across model families or training on another model's synthetic output.
claims.source: Tuhin Chakrabarty, Philippe Laban et al., Salesforce AI Research, arXiv:2409.14509, September 2024
claims.quote: all 3 LLMs generate these idiosyncratic words/phrases

claims.claim: The study found that none of the three LLMs it used outperformed each other in terms of writing quality, which it reads as common limitations across model families.
claims.source: Tuhin Chakrabarty, Philippe Laban et al., Salesforce AI Research, arXiv:2409.14509, September 2024
claims.quote: none of the LLMs used in our study

claims.claim: In the study's taxonomy, edits in the Lack of Specificity and Detail category typically make the text longer, because writers add detail rather than cut.
claims.source: Tuhin Chakrabarty, Philippe Laban et al., Salesforce AI Research, arXiv:2409.14509, September 2024
claims.quote: typically make the text longer as writers add more details
claims.page: Section 4.4.5, Lack of Specificity and Detail

claims.claim: One professional writer in the study, identified as W1, reported that a very common phrasing in the LLM excerpts was seem to plus a verb, which the writer judged inelegant and preferred replaced by the plain verb.
claims.source: Writer W1, quoted from an email in Chakrabarty, Laban et al., arXiv:2409.14509, September 2024
claims.quote: a very common phrasing in these excerpts is
claims.page: Section 4.4.6, Awkward Word Choice and Phrasing

claims.claim: The study's large-scale preference annotation found that experts largely prefer text edited by other experts over automatically edited text.
claims.source: Tuhin Chakrabarty, Philippe Laban et al., Salesforce AI Research, arXiv:2409.14509, September 2024
claims.quote: although experts largely prefer text edited by other experts

claims.claim: In the study's span-detection evaluation, expert agreement with each other on which spans are problematic reached only 0.57 general precision and 0.23 categorical precision.
claims.source: Tuhin Chakrabarty, Philippe Laban et al., Salesforce AI Research, arXiv:2409.14509, September 2024

claims.claim: Mollick argues that badly prompted AI writing produces very little meaning per word and takes the reader in intellectual circles.

claims.quote: produces very little meaning per word, taking you in intellectual circles

claims.feature: other: surface polish with nothing underneath

verdicts.trueWording: Table 8 row 1: DT NN IN NN CC, 54% of times edited
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of arxiv.org/html/2409.14509v3 fetched with a browser UA (HTTP 200) and stripped to text. Table 8's first row reads 'DT NN IN NN CC | 54% | a mix of pride and, a mix of fear and, a sense of protection and, a sense of wonder and, ...' under the column header '% of Times Edited'; caption: 'Idiosyncratic Sequences ... that are edited by writers'. Both named representative sequences are present. Graded SUBSTANCE only because the claim supplies no quotation to match word for word; every limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: a word like unspoken occurs in about 15% of LLM-generated responses
verdicts.note: Section 5.3 (inside section 5, 'The LAMP Corpus'): 'For instance, Figure 6 shows how a word like unspoken occurs in about 15% of LLM-generated responses.' Quote appears word for word; Figure 6's caption confirms the LAMP Corpus scope.

verdicts.trueWording: occur very rarely or not at all in original seed paragraphs
verdicts.note: Section 5.3: 'Similarly phrases such as weight of, sense of, mix of occur very rarely or not at all in original seed paragraphs (Table 1) while they occur frequently in LLM-generated responses.' The 'human-written' limb is carried by the paper's own wording elsewhere ('the original seed human-written paragraphs (Table 1)'; Table 8 caption 'the human written seed paragraphs'). No quotation was supplied, hence SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM.

verdicts.trueWording: all 3 LLMs generate these idiosyncratic words/phrases
verdicts.note: Section 5.3: 'The most surprising finding is that all 3 LLMs generate these idiosyncratic words/phrases suggesting possible overlap/mixture in instruction tuning data across model families or one model trained on synthetic data generated from another model (Zhou et al., 2024).' Quote verbatim; both suggested causes match.

verdicts.trueWording: none of the LLMs used in our study ... outperform each other
verdicts.note: Abstract: 'Analysis of LAMP reveals that none of the LLMs used in our study (GPT4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Llama-3.1-70b) outperform each other in terms of writing quality, revealing common limitations across model families.' Quote verbatim; exactly three LLMs are named, and the 'common limitations across model families' limb is the paper's own reading.

verdicts.trueWording: typically make the text longer as writers add more details
verdicts.note: Section 4.4.5 'Lack of Specificity and Detail': 'Edits belonging to this category typically make the text longer as writers add more details to make the text engaging.' Quote verbatim; 'rather than cut' is a gloss entailed by the page's own longer-because-added-details statement, not a separate assertion.

verdicts.trueWording: a very common phrasing in these excerpts is 'seem to _(verb)_'
verdicts.note: Section 4.4.6 'Awkward Word Choice and Phrasing': 'In an email W1 pointed out “Another little observation to share: a very common phrasing in these excerpts is ‘seem to _(verb)_’. This is not technically wrong it’s just inelegant ... it’s always preferred to just use the verb without ‘seem’ (ex. ... ‘amplified’ is better than ‘seemed to amplify’)”.' Quote verbatim; email attribution, W1, inelegance and the plain-verb preference are all on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: although experts largely prefer text edited by other experts
verdicts.note: Abstract: 'A large-scale preference annotation confirms that although experts largely prefer text edited by other experts, automatic editing methods show promise in improving alignment...'. Quote verbatim; the 'over automatically edited text' limb is supported by section 6's description of the study as 'comparing human and LLM-produced edits'.

Section 6.1, Table 9: row 'Expert Agreement | 0.57 | 0.23' under headers 'General Precision' and 'Categorical Precision'; body text confirms 'the expert agreement level (0.57)' and that the 50 independently edited paragraphs were used 'to estimate expert-expert agreement'. No quotation supplied, hence SUBSTANCE. Note the 0.23 figure additionally requires correct category assignment, not span identification alone.
